title: Mole Poblano
description: Chicken simmered in a deep, toasted-chilli and Mexican-chocolate sauce from Puebla — savoury first, with only a whisper of sweetness once it's finished cooking down.

ingredients.item: dried ancho chillies, stemmed and seeded
ingredients.note: or wide dried chilli pods from a Kapitan Chinatown or online Mexican-goods seller; do not substitute fresh chilli

ingredients.item: dried guajillo chillies, stemmed and seeded
ingredients.note: sold locally as 'dried red chillies' in some Asian groceries, but the real guajillo is worth ordering online

ingredients.item: dried pasilla chillies, stemmed and seeded
ingredients.note: if unavailable, use 2 more ancho and add 1/4 tsp smoked paprika

ingredients.item: sesame seeds, plus extra for garnish

ingredients.note: or a very ripe saba banana, which is closer in starch to Mexican plantain than a cavendish
true Ceylon cinnamon (canela) if you can find it; ordinary cassia cinnamon works but is stronger, use less
or dark chocolate 70% plus a pinch of ground cinnamon and cloves as a stand-in

ingredients.item: lard or neutral oil, for frying

ingredients.note: to taste

steps: Combine the chicken, water, onion and garlic in a large pot, bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer 35 minutes until the chicken is just cooked. Lift out the chicken and strain the broth; set both aside.

Wipe the dried chillies clean and toast them a few at a time in a dry skillet, pressing flat, until fragrant and the flesh turns tobacco-brown, about 20 seconds a side — do not let them blacken or the sauce turns bitter. Soak the toasted chillies in 2 cups of the hot broth.
In the same skillet with a little lard, fry the raisins until plump, the almonds until golden, and the sesame seeds until they pop; drain each onto a plate.
Fry the tortilla and plantain slices in the same skillet until browned, then add to the same plate along with the roasted tomatoes.
Working in batches, blend the soaked chillies with their broth, the fried ingredients, cinnamon and 1 cup fresh broth until completely smooth; strain if any grit remains.
Heat the remaining lard in a wide pot, pour in the blended sauce, and fry it down, stirring constantly, until it darkens and thickens, about 10 minutes.
Stir in the chocolate and enough broth to reach a gravy-like consistency, then simmer uncovered 25–30 minutes, stirring often to stop it catching, until the surface shows small pools of oil.
Season with salt, slide in the cooked chicken pieces, and simmer 10 minutes more until heated through. Serve over the chicken with a sprinkle of sesame seeds, plain white rice and warm tortillas.
tips: This is a genuine weekend project — 3 separately toasted components and a two-stage blend — but the sauce freezes beautifully for 3 months, so it's worth doubling.
Toast the chillies in small batches; if the kitchen fills with sharp smoke, they've scorched and will taste bitter no matter how much chocolate you add.
kidNote: The finished mole is mild and rounded, not hot; the kids can eat the same plate as the adults. If they're chilli-averse, spoon their portion before you check it for salt and add nothing further.
nutritionNote: Rich in fat from the nuts, seeds and lard used to build the sauce; balance the plate with plain rice and a simple salad rather than more fried sides.

title: Chiles en Nogada
description: Roasted poblano chillies stuffed with a sweet-savoury picadillo of pork, fruit and spice, draped in a fresh walnut cream and finished with pomegranate — Mexico's flag on a plate.

ingredients.note: look for the long, dark-green 'pasilla bilbo'-style chilli sold in specialty grocers; a mild long green finger chilli can stand in but roast very briefly since it's thinner
or a very ripe saba banana
queso de cabra shops and some Landmark/Santis branches carry shelled walnuts; soak them in milk overnight to loosen the papery skin for a whiter sauce
pomegranates appear in PH supermarkets around September–November; if out of season, use halved red grapes for the colour and let the dish rest until pomegranate returns

steps: Roast the poblanos directly over a flame or under a broiler, turning until the skin blisters and blackens all over, then seal in a plastic bag for 10 minutes to steam.
Peel off the blackened skin under running water, then slit each chilli down one side and remove the seeds, keeping the stem intact. Set aside.
For the filling, brown the pork and beef in a wide pan, then add the onion and garlic and cook until soft.
Stir in the tomatoes, plantain, apple, pear, raisins, almonds and cinnamon; simmer uncovered 15 minutes until thick and no longer wet, then season with salt and let cool slightly.
For the sauce, blend the walnuts, cream cheese, milk and sugar until completely smooth; season with a pinch of salt.
Stuff each chilli generously with the warm filling, reshaping it closed around the meat.
Plate the stuffed chillies, spoon the walnut sauce generously over the top so the chilli barely shows, and scatter with pomegranate seeds and parsley.
Serve immediately at room temperature — this dish is not meant to be served hot.
tips: This is the most labour-intensive dish in the file: budget a full afternoon. The chillies, filling and sauce can each be made up to 2 days ahead and only assembled at the table.
Soaking the walnuts in milk overnight and slipping off the thin skins by hand is what keeps the sauce ivory-white instead of grey — don't skip it for a special occasion.
kidNote: There's no chilli heat in this dish at all; poblano is a mild pepper once roasted. Dice a portion of the filling small for younger kids so it's easier to manage with a fork.
nutritionNote: A rich, occasion dish — cream cheese and walnuts carry a lot of fat, so serve smaller portions with a plain green salad rather than more sides.

title: Birria de Res
description: Beef shank and chuck braised for hours in a toasted-chilli adobo until it falls apart, served shredded in its own deep red broth with onion, cilantro and lime.

ingredients.item: beef chuck and shank, cut into large chunks
dried guajillo chillies, stemmed and seeded
ingredients.note: order online from a Mexican-goods seller if not stocked locally

ingredients.item: dried ancho chillies, stemmed and seeded

ingredients.note: omit or halve for a milder broth; siling labuyo is a reasonable stand-in for heat only, not flavour

steps: Toast the guajillo, ancho and árbol chillies in a dry skillet a few seconds per side until fragrant, then soak them in hot water for 15 minutes to soften.
Char the tomatoes, onion and garlic in the same dry skillet until spotted black in places.
Blend the soaked chillies, charred vegetables, oregano, cumin, cinnamon, cloves and vinegar with 1 cup of the soaking water until completely smooth; strain to remove any skins.
Season the beef chunks with salt and sear in a heavy pot until browned on all sides.
Pour the chilli adobo over the beef, add the bay leaves and broth, and bring to a boil.
Cover, reduce heat to low, and simmer gently 2.5–3 hours, until the beef shreds easily with a fork.
Lift out the beef and shred it, skimming excess fat from the surface of the broth, then return the shredded meat to the pot to heat through.
Ladle into bowls with plenty of broth and serve with chopped onion, cilantro and lime wedges on the side.
tips: Birria is even better the next day once the chillies have had time to mellow into the broth — make it a day ahead if you can.
The fat that rises to the top of the broth is traditionally kept for dipping tortillas (quesabirria); skim only what you don't want.
kidNote: The chilli de árbol carries most of the heat — leave it out of the pot entirely for a family batch and pass a small dish of toasted chilli flakes or hot sauce at the table for adults who want it spicier.
nutritionNote: A protein-forward, long-cooked dish; serve with warm corn tortillas and a squeeze of lime, and add a side of sautéed greens since the meal itself has no vegetables beyond the broth base.

title: Pozole Verde
description: Guerrero-style hominy soup in a bright tomatillo, poblano and pumpkin-seed broth with tender pork — a completely different pot from red pozole, herbal and tangy rather than deep and dried-chilli-based.

ingredients.item: pork shoulder, cut into large chunks
white onion, half quartered and half finely chopped

ingredients.note: canned hominy is sold in a few specialty Asian/Western grocers in Manila; dried hominy soaked and boiled overnight is the closer substitute if you can't find it
look for fresh tomatillo at specialty produce stalls or use canned tomatillo; in a pinch, substitute unripe green tomatoes plus extra lime juice for tartness
siling haba works, though it's milder — add a whole siling labuyo per person's taste if you want more heat
to taste

steps: Simmer the pork with the quartered onion and 2 garlic cloves in the water for about 1 hour, skimming foam, until the meat is tender. Strain and reserve the broth; keep the pork in a bowl.
Boil the tomatillos, poblanos and serranos in a separate small pot of water for 8 minutes until soft, then drain.
Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry skillet, stirring constantly, until they puff and start to pop, then set aside to cool.
Blend the boiled tomatillos, poblanos, serranos, remaining garlic, half the toasted pumpkin seeds, cilantro and romaine leaves with a cup of the reserved broth until smooth.
Heat the oil in a wide pot and fry the green purée for about 5 minutes, stirring often, until it darkens slightly and smells cooked rather than raw.
Add the remaining broth, the hominy and the cooked pork; simmer uncovered 20 minutes so the flavors come together.
Grind the remaining pumpkin seeds and stir half into the pot to thicken the broth slightly; taste and season with salt.
Ladle into bowls and let everyone garnish their own with chopped onion, radish, shredded cabbage, oregano, lime and the remaining ground pumpkin seeds.
tips: Fry the blended green sauce properly before adding broth — this step, called 'frying the base', is what stops pozole verde from tasting raw and grassy.
kidNote: The serrano chillies give this a real kick — for the kids' bowls, ladle broth before the chillies are blended in, or simply serve theirs with no chilli-forward garnish and keep sliced fresh chilli as a table topping for adults.
nutritionNote: Hominy and pumpkin seeds make this a good source of fibre alongside the pork protein; skim excess fat from the pork broth before serving to keep it lighter.

title: Caldo Tlalpeño
description: A light, smoky chicken and chickpea soup from Mexico City, scented with a whole chipotle and topped with avocado and cheese — the everyday soup on every fonda menu.

ingredients.note: canned chickpeas, drained, are the easiest local option

ingredients.item: green beans, cut into short lengths

ingredients.note: epazote is rarely sold locally; use a small handful of cilantro instead, added at the end, for a fresher though less pungent finish
or a mild farmer's cheese; kesong puti is a good local match
sold canned in some supermarket Mexican/international aisles; keep it whole so the broth stays mild and diners spoon out as much smoky heat as they want

steps: Heat the oil in a soup pot and sauté the onion and garlic until soft.
Add the blended tomato and cook 3–4 minutes, stirring, until it deepens in color and smells cooked rather than raw.
Pour in the chicken broth, add the chicken thighs, carrot and epazote (or hold the cilantro for later), and bring to a boil.
Reduce heat and simmer, partially covered, 20 minutes until the chicken is cooked through.
Lift out the chicken, shred the meat off the bone, and return the shredded meat to the pot along with the chickpeas and green beans.
Simmer 8–10 more minutes until the green beans are tender, then stir in the cilantro if using instead of epazote and season with salt.
Ladle into bowls and top each with avocado slices and crumbled cheese.
Add the whole chipotle to the pot at the table, or slice into individual bowls only for diners who want the smoky heat.
kidNote: Keep the chipotle whole and out of the broth until serving so the base stays completely mild; the kids can eat straight from the pot without it.
nutritionNote: A well-balanced one-bowl meal — lean chicken, chickpeas and vegetables in a light broth — that needs nothing more than warm tortillas alongside.

title: Sopa de Lima
description: A Yucatecan chicken soup perfumed with sour lima citrus and a light tomato-pepper sofrito, finished with crisp fried tortilla strips for crunch.

ingredients.note: Yucatecan lima fruit isn't sold here; use fresh calamansi or a mix of lime and a little orange zest for the same sour-floral note
labuyo is far hotter per gram than habanero but similar in kick — use half a piece, kept whole, and taste before adding more

steps: Simmer the chicken thighs in the broth for 25 minutes until cooked through, then lift out, shred the meat, and set the broth aside.
Heat the oil in a soup pot and sauté the onion and bell pepper until soft, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook 1 minute, then stir in the tomatoes and oregano and cook until the tomatoes break down, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the reserved broth and bring to a simmer for 10 minutes so the flavors combine.
Return the shredded chicken to the pot and stir in the lima or calamansi juice; taste and adjust the sourness and salt.
Meanwhile, fry the tortilla strips in hot oil until golden and crisp, then drain on paper towels.
Drop the whole habanero into the pot just before serving for aroma without heat, and remove it before ladling if no one wants it fiery.
Ladle the soup into bowls and top with crisp tortilla strips and avocado slices.
kidNote: The habanero stays whole and unbroken in the broth purely for aroma; fish it out before serving the kids their bowls so there's no risk of it bursting into their portion.
nutritionNote: A light broth-based soup with lean chicken and vegetables; the fried tortilla strips add most of the fat, so go easy on those for a lighter bowl.

title: Aguachile Verde
description: Raw shrimp quick-cured in lime juice and a blended serrano-cilantro salsa, tossed with cucumber, red onion and avocado — Sinaloa's fierier, punchier cousin of ceviche.

ingredients.item: raw shrimp, peeled, deveined and halved lengthwise
ingredients.note: buy the freshest shrimp you can from the wet market or a seafood counter, since it is eaten raw
siling haba is milder; use siling labuyo instead if you want the real Sinaloa heat

ingredients.item: tostadas or tortilla chips, for serving

steps: Lay the shrimp in a shallow glass or ceramic dish and pour over 1 cup of the lime juice with the salt. Cover and refrigerate 30 minutes, flipping halfway, until the shrimp turns pink and opaque.
While the shrimp cures, blend the serrano chillies, cilantro and remaining lime juice until smooth.
Drain a little of the curing lime juice from the shrimp, then pour the green chilli marinade over the top and toss gently to coat.
Cover and refrigerate a further 30 minutes so the flavors combine.
Just before serving, fold in the red onion and cucumber.
Arrange on a platter topped with avocado slices and serve immediately with tostadas or tortilla chips on the side.
tips: Use a glass or ceramic dish, never metal — the lime juice reacts with metal and gives the shrimp a tinny off-flavor.
Slicing the shrimp in half lengthwise lets it cure through in the same time it takes the surface to turn opaque, so nothing is left raw in the middle.
kidNote: This is a genuinely hot, raw-cured adult dish — not recommended for the kids. Make a plain shrimp cocktail (cooked shrimp, ketchup-lime sauce, no chilli) for their plates from the same bag of shrimp instead.
nutritionNote: Lean and high in protein with almost no added fat; the sodium comes mostly from salt and the acid from lime, so it pairs well with a starch like tostadas to round out the meal.

title: Pescado Zarandeado
description: A whole butterflied fish marinated in a smoky chile-citrus sauce and grilled over open flame until charred and flaky — Nayarit's classic beachside centerpiece.

ingredients.item: whole red snapper or similar white fish, butterflied and cleaned
ingredients.note: ask the wet market to butterfly it for you; maya-maya (mangrove red snapper) or lapu-lapu are good local substitutes

ingredients.item: dried guajillo chillies, stemmed and seeded
ingredients.note: order online from a Mexican-goods seller if unavailable locally

ingredients.item: dried ancho chillies, stemmed and seeded

ingredients.note: sold in Latin-goods sections or online; if unavailable, use 1 tsp paprika plus a pinch of turmeric for the color
to taste

steps: Toast the dried guajillo and ancho chillies in a dry skillet a few seconds per side until fragrant, then soak in hot water for 15 minutes until soft.
Blend the soaked chillies with the garlic, orange juice, lime juice, soy sauce, mayonnaise, mustard, achiote paste, oil and salt until completely smooth.
Lay the butterflied fish skin-side down and spread the marinade generously over the flesh, working it into the slashes. Cover and refrigerate at least 1 hour, or up to overnight.
Heat a charcoal grill to medium-high, or heat a large griddle indoors if grilling isn't possible.
Grill the fish flesh-side down first for 6–8 minutes until char marks form, then carefully flip to the skin side.
Continue grilling skin-side down for another 10–12 minutes, basting with any remaining marinade, until the fish flakes easily with a fork.
Transfer to a platter and serve whole with warm corn tortillas, sliced onion and lime wedges.
tips: A fish basket or two wire racks tied together makes flipping a whole butterflied fish over open coals far easier and keeps it from falling apart.
No grill? A very hot oven broiler with the fish on a sheet pan gets close, though you'll miss the smoke.
kidNote: The marinade has only mild warmth from the dried chillies with no fresh heat added, so it should suit the kids as-is; if they're sensitive, scrape a little of the marinade off their portion before serving.
nutritionNote: A lean, high-protein main; the mayonnaise in the marinade adds richness, so balance the plate with rice and a simple vegetable side rather than more sauce.

title: Nopales con Huevo
description: Scrambled eggs cooked with tender cactus paddles, onion and garlic — a everyday Mexican breakfast that's earthy, a little tangy, and ready before the coffee finishes brewing.

ingredients.item: nopales (cactus paddles), cleaned, diced, and boiled until tender
ingredients.note: fresh nopales are rare here; jarred nopalitos (sold in some Latin/import grocers) are a fair swap — rinse well to cut the brine before using
to taste
to taste
kesong puti works well as a mild local substitute

steps: Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat.
Add the onion and garlic and cook, stirring, for 3 minutes until the onion is soft and translucent.
Add the cooked nopales and cook 3 more minutes, stirring occasionally.
Pour in the beaten eggs and cook, stirring gently every 10 seconds, until light, fluffy and just set.
Season with salt and pepper and remove from heat immediately so the eggs don't overcook.
Serve hot, topped with crumbled cheese, with warm tortillas alongside.
tips: Stir gently and pull the pan off the heat a beat early — the eggs keep cooking in residual heat and go rubbery fast if left in the pan too long.
If using jarred nopalitos, pat them very dry after rinsing so the eggs don't turn watery.
nutritionNote: A high-protein, fibre-rich breakfast from the nopales; pair with beans and tortillas for a fuller, more balanced meal.

title: Arroz con Leche
description: Rice slow-simmered in cinnamon-scented milk until thick and creamy — a simple, gently sweet Mexican rice pudding that's just as good warm as it is chilled.

ingredients.note: true Ceylon canela if available; ordinary cassia cinnamon sticks work fine too

ingredients.item: ground cinnamon and chopped nuts or raisins, for topping
ingredients.note: optional

steps: Combine the water, rice, cinnamon sticks and salt in a large pot over medium-high heat.
Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low, cover, and cook 15 minutes until the water is mostly absorbed.
Stir in the milk and sugar and bring back to a gentle boil.
Reduce heat to low and cook uncovered 25–30 minutes, stirring often, until the pudding has thickened to a loose, creamy consistency.
Remove the cinnamon sticks and serve warm in bowls, or refrigerate 2 hours and serve cold.
Garnish with a dusting of ground cinnamon and chopped nuts or raisins if desired.
tips: Stir often once the milk goes in — rice scorches easily on the bottom of the pot and will taste burnt through the whole batch if it catches.
nutritionNote: A sugar- and dairy-forward dessert; a small bowl is plenty for kids, and it pairs well as a light finish after a vegetable-heavy main rather than another rich dish.
